newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Lloyds' chair says insurers need client focus.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Lloyds' chair says insurers need client focus.

text.p: Lloyds of London chairman David Rowland said on Friday he was concerned about the outlook for the commercial insurance industry because it was losing business due to a lack of customer focus.
"I worry about our industry because of our failure to relate properly to the needs of our clients," Rowland said at a luncheon hosted by the Australia-British Chamber of Commerce.
He said the risk transfer industry was poaching about US$50 billion of business from the commercial insurance market every year.

"Part of our problem in the insurance business is that we are only now doing a portion of the trade that our predecessors actually did and we have got to try and think our way back to getting more of that back into our business," he said in response to question.

Customers started taking their insurance business elsewhere in the late 1960's by forming captives - companies that insure their own risks - and this was driven by the perception that it was much cheaper to tap the reinsurance market than use the commercial insurance market, Rowland said.
"Those were the early signs, many other self insurance moves have happened since then."
Earlier, Rowland said the rescue plan for Lloyd's, which won the support of 94.3 percent of its member in September, meant the organisation could now go forward.
Under the plan, Lloyd's reinsured 14.7 billion stg in past liabilities into a new company, Equitas.

The plan ended years of uncertainty over the scale of massive losses suffered by some Lloyd's investors as a result of unlimited liability to past claims, including those relating to U.S. environmental and asbestosis insurance.
"(the plan ensured) that Lloyd's for 1993/94, properly capitalised, properly reserved, would go forward to a future which I think is every bit enticing as ever its past was."

Rowland also said there was no guarantee for the survival of an insurance market like Lloyd's of London, but that he believed Lloyd's would thrive because of the personal contact customers had with its brokers and underwriters.
"They are able to look that man in the eye and know that he is actually making the decision and know that he is backing himself, his own personal money in it too," Rowland said.
Lloyd's problems started in the 1980s, when a string of natural disasters, negligent underwriting and a reinsurance spiral led to more than 8.0 billion stg in losses from 1988 to 1992.
Since 1995, Equitas has paid up to three billion stg in claims and an audit of the company will be completed by the end of this year.
